data.content_ref: inline:SRC_003 argues the panel is more reliable by replacing high-variance expert peaks with a high-floor baseline, but it does not establish that this higher floor is genuine reliability rather than mere compliance that tracks the right answer on the evaluated items. Raising the floor only shows the panel avoids catastrophic slips; it does not, within a single evaluation, distinguish a panel that genuinely verified each item from one that compliance-ticked the same items and happened to be correct because the checklist happened to match the outcome. The problem explicitly demands this distinction, and the variance-reduction mechanism does not supply it: low variance can come from uniform compliance just as easily as from uniform genuine verification. The analogy to surgical safety checklists does not close the gap because the target itself flags that those checklists are used by experts, not non-experts, so the transfer claim that the floor-raising is genuine (not mere compliance) is unsupported for the non-expert panel the problem concerns.
